The hidden mathematics of crystal growth

Published 2026-10-05 05:30 UTC

A snowflake's six arms grow in strikingly regular patterns, yet no two flakes look exactly alike. Explaining that combination of order and variety has occupied mathematicians and physicists for centuries. Recent work is revealing the equations that govern how crystals grow and why their shapes are so diverse.

Crystal growth is controlled by how quickly molecules attach to different faces of the crystal. In a snowflake, water vapor diffuses through the air and sticks to the growing ice. Tips that stick out slightly gather vapor faster than the surrounding surface, so they grow faster still. This instability creates branches, while the crystal's underlying hexagonal structure keeps them aligned.

Mathematical models capture this process with equations that describe diffusion and the rate at which molecules join the surface. Small changes in temperature and humidity change those rates, which is why snowflakes falling through different air layers develop different shapes. Computer simulations based on these models now reproduce many forms seen in nature.

Quasicrystals add another twist. Discovered in the 1980s, they are ordered but never repeat, with symmetries once thought impossible for crystals. Mathematicians have connected their structures to tilings of the plane that never repeat, and to projections of regular lattices from higher dimensions.

Researchers are using these insights to grow materials with useful properties, from semiconductors with fewer defects to pharmaceutical crystals that dissolve at the right rate. Controlling the conditions of growth can determine which crystal form appears, which matters because different forms of the same drug can behave very differently in the body.

Despite the progress, some questions remain open, including how impurities alter growth patterns in ways that models struggle to predict.

Researchers in materials science are building on these models with experiments in microgravity, where the absence of convection lets crystals grow under purely diffusive conditions that are easier to compare with theory.
